layers.name: The number on the page
layers.what: This layer is the pages' own JavaScript, not R or Python; the R code starts at layer 3. The overview page reads the explorer's grid file and prints the NBER entry of its preferred list as the headline: the printed mean NPV, -38.9, as '-$38.9B'. The explorer does the same when its dials sit at the NBER setting; at any other setting it prints the grid's exact expectation for that setting instead, and a small line under the number says which of the two it shows.
layers.inputs: G = window.__GRID__ from grid.js: G.preferred (the authors' two settings) and G.snap (every setting)

inputs_from.what: G = window.__GRID__: G.preferred holds the printed and rerun means of the two versions

layers.other_inputs: the dial positions on screen; the page opens on the NBER setting [0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0]
layers.outputs: the text '−$38.9B' under 'Main estimate, NBER September 2026'
layers.method_ref: Display only. The definition under the number is the method: NPV = WT - f.C/r, averaged over the authors' Monte Carlo draws. Footnote 1 says it is the authors' own headline (NBER PDF p.1).

r.symbol: the headline block and its script
r.snippet:
Main estimate1, NBER September 2026 −$38.9B Defined as the one-time wealth tax revenue minus the present value of California income tax lost for ever to billionaires who leave, averaged over 100,000 random runs of the authors' model (a Monte Carlo simulation). Today's dollars (present value): what money received or lost in future years is worth now.

The loss decides the sign. The income tax lost for ever is worth about $75B today, against $36B, the average wealth tax in the authors' simulation (their own estimate of what is collected is about $30B; what the model says).

1 Jaros and Rauh, NBER chapter c15504, Tax Policy and the Economy vol. 41, PDF p.1. The figure is the average of one seeded run of the authors' simulation (a run started from a fixed random number, so it gives the same draws every time). It revises a March 2026 first version by Rauh, Jaros, Kearney, Doran and Cosso (footnote 2).

layers.name: Writing the grid file
layers.what: Turns the grid table and the headline table into the text of grid.js. The preferred list is built here: for each version it copies the printed mean, page and share negative from the headline table, and the seeded rerun's mean rounded to three decimals (mc_npv = -38.886). The snap rows are the grid's four outcomes rounded to three decimals. The Python twin never produces this file: it exports its own parallel CSVs (export/py/outputs.csv), which layer 4 checks against the R output for parity, but the JavaScript grid file itself is generated once, by R only.
layers.inputs: the grid table (2,187 rows), the revenue chain (for the dial labels) and the headline table

inputs_from.what: site_grid: one row per dial combination, the exact expectation in mean_npv

layers.other_inputs: the dial definitions and the two named settings (site_dials(), site_named())
layers.outputs: the text of grid.js, written to site/explorer/grid.js

r.snippet:
# ---- grid.js writer ---------------------------------------------------------
site_grid_payload <- function(site_grid, revenue_chain, site_headlines) {
  dials <- site_dials(revenue_chain)
  named <- site_named()
  outcome_cols <- c("mean_npv", "pct_negative", "wt_collected", "pv_lost")
  hl <- function(v, qn, col) site_headlines[[col]][site_headlines$version == v & site_headlines$quantity == qn]
  # Printed values exist only for the two published versions.
  pref <- lapply(intersect(names(named), unique(site_headlines$version)), function(v) list(
    key = v, label = unname(site_named_labels()[v]),
    printed_npv = hl(v, "mc_mean_npv", "printed"),
    printed_pct_negative = hl(v, "mc_pct_negative", "printed"),
    printed_revenue = hl(v, "revenue_headline", "printed"),
    printed_page = hl(v, "mc_mean_npv", "printed_page"),
    mc_npv = round(hl(v, "mc_mean_npv", "reproduced"), 3),
    mc_pct_negative = round(hl(v, "mc_pct_negative", "reproduced"), 3)
  ))
  list(
    generated_by = "rjkdc-analysis/R/site.R::write_site_grid_js() via targets (target site_grid_js); do not edit by hand",
    dials = lapply(dials, function(d) list(key = d$key, sym = d$sym, label = d$label, origin = d$origin,
                                           desc = d$desc, tips = d$tips, more = d$more,
                                           labels = d$labels, levels = seq_along(d$labels) - 1L)),
    outcomes = c("Mean NPV, exact average", "Share of outcomes with NPV below zero, exact",
                 "Expected wealth tax collected", "Expected present value of lost income tax"),
    units = c("$B", "%", "$B", "$B"),
    named = lapply(named, function(x) unname(as.integer(x))),
    named_labels = as.list(site_named_labels()),
    preferred = pref,
    snap = unname(lapply(seq_len(nrow(site_grid)), function(i)
      round(unlist(site_grid[i, outcome_cols]), 3)))
  )
}

write_site_grid_js <- function(site_grid, revenue_chain, site_headlines,
                               path = "site/explorer/grid.js") {
  payload <- site_grid_payload(site_grid, revenue_chain, site_headlines)

  dir.create(dirname(path), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  writeLines(c(
    "/* GENERATED FILE: written by rjkdc-analysis/R/site.R::write_site_grid_js()",
    "   (targets: site_grid_js). Do not edit by hand; tests/testthat/test-site.R",
    "   fails if this file differs from the exporter's own output. */",

layers.name: The headline table
layers.what: One row per number either paper prints, beside the pipeline's value for it. The NBER mean NPV row takes the printed -38.9 (typed from PDF p.1 and p.35, with its page), the seeded Monte Carlo's mean (layer 5) as 'reproduced', and the grid's exact expectation for the NBER setting (layer 6) as 'grid_exact'. The R code below is the function definition; it is called and assigned to the site_headlines target in _targets.R:66-69 (tar_target(site_headlines, compute_site_headlines(...))), the same call the Pipeline line points to. Correction, 2026-10-27: this layer previously said the Python twin builds the same rows in export/py/outputs.csv. It does not. site_headlines (this table, with its quantity/printed/reproduced/grid_exact columns) feeds grid.js (layer 3) and has no Python twin, the same as grid.js itself (layer 3's note). Python's build_outputs() (py/run_export.py) is a different, broader table, keyed by output_id and printed_value, and its real R twin is compute_export_outputs() in R/export.R, which writes export/r/outputs.csv: a separate export the materials page's own parity test checks against export/py/outputs.csv (materials.qmd, test kind 3), outside this chain. build_outputs() does include the NBER mean NPV as one of its rows (npv_mc_nber_mean), computed independently from the same Monte Carlo (layer 5), which is why a reader can be misled into treating it as this layer's twin.

inputs_from.what: npv_mc_nber_summary: the seeded run's mean, median, SD and share negative

layers.name: The seeded Monte Carlo (the printed number)
layers.what: The authors' NBER script, ported line by line. It sets the seed 2026, draws four inputs 100,000 times in a fixed order (revenue WT on [0, 72], the departure share f on [0.30, 0.60], the annual income tax C on [3.3, 5.8], the discount rate on [0.015, 0.045]), computes NPV = WT - f.C/r for each draw and averages. Because R's random stream and the draw order are the authors', the mean is theirs to machine precision: -38.886, printed -38.9. This is the last layer that computes the headline. The Python twin runs the same algorithm on numpy's random stream, so its mean differs within Monte Carlo error.
layers.inputs: the draw ranges, as the function's defaults

inputs_from.what: the draw ranges: WT 0 to 72, f 0.30 to 0.60, C 3.3 to 5.8, r 0.015 to 0.045

layers.outputs: summary$mean = -38.886348 (printed -38.9); median, SD and share negative beside it
layers.method_ref: NBER PDF p.35 (eq. 16) and the authors' NPV_dist_v8.R. Matches: test-npv-mc.R runs the authors' script unmodified and checks every one of the 100,000 NPVs equals ours to 1e-9, and checks the mean against the printed -38.9 within four Monte Carlo standard errors.

r.snippet:
compute_npv_mc_nber <- function(seed = 2026, n_sims = 100000,
                                 wt_min = 0, wt_max = 72,
                                 f_min = 0.30, f_max = 0.60,
                                 c_min = 3.3, c_max = 5.8,
                                 rg_min = 0.015, rg_max = 0.045) {
  set.seed(seed)
  wt <- stats::runif(n_sims, wt_min, wt_max)
  f  <- stats::runif(n_sims, f_min, f_max)
  c_income <- stats::runif(n_sims, c_min, c_max)
  rg_discount <- stats::runif(n_sims, rg_min, rg_max)

  npv <- wt - (f * c_income) / rg_discount

  list(
    draws = tibble::tibble(wt = wt, f = f, c_income = c_income,
                            rg_discount = rg_discount, npv = npv),
    summary = npv_mc_summary(npv)
  )
}

npv_mc_summary <- function(npv) {
  tibble::tibble(
    n = length(npv),
    mean = mean(npv),
    median = stats::median(npv),
    sd = stats::sd(npv),
    p05 = unname(stats::quantile(npv, 0.05)),
    p95 = unname(stats::quantile(npv, 0.95)),
    min = min(npv),
    max = max(npv),
    pct_negative = 100 * mean(npv < 0)

py.snippet:
def compute_npv_mc_nber(seed=2026, n_sims=100000, wt_min=0, wt_max=72,
                         f_min=0.30, f_max=0.60, c_min=3.3, c_max=5.8,
                         rg_min=0.015, rg_max=0.045):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    wt = rng.uniform(wt_min, wt_max, n_sims)
    f = rng.uniform(f_min, f_max, n_sims)
    c_income = rng.uniform(c_min, c_max, n_sims)
    rg_discount = rng.uniform(rg_min, rg_max, n_sims)

    npv = wt - (f * c_income) / rg_discount
    return {"npv": npv, "summary": npv_mc_summary(npv)}


def npv_mc_summary(npv):
    return {
        "n": len(npv),
        "mean": float(np.mean(npv)),
        "median": float(np.median(npv)),
        "sd": float(np.std(npv, ddof=1)),
        "p05": float(np.percentile(npv, 5)),
        "p95": float(np.percentile(npv, 95)),
        "min": float(np.min(npv)),
        "max": float(np.max(npv)),

layers.name: The exact expectation (the explorer's cells)
layers.what: The four draws are independent, so the average NPV has a closed form: E[WT] - E[f] x E[C] x E[1/r], with E[1/r] = ln(0.045/0.015)/0.03 = 36.62. At the NBER ranges that is 36 - 0.45 x 4.55 x 36.62 = 36 - 74.98 = -38.98. The explorer's 2,187 cells all come from this function, so moving a dial needs no new random draw. The headline itself is the seeded run (layer 5); this layer is the cross-check beside it and the value the explorer shows away from the authors' settings.
layers.inputs: the same draw ranges as layer 5

inputs_from.what: the draw ranges: WT 0 to 72, f 0.30 to 0.60, C 3.3 to 5.8, r 0.015 to 0.045

layers.other_inputs: f_spec = list(mode = 'uniform', lo = 0.30, hi = 0.60); q = 1 and g = 0 as coded
layers.method_ref: Expectation of a product of independent variables is the product of their expectations; E[1/r] for r uniform on [a, b] is ln(b/a)/(b - a). test-site.R checks the grid cell equals npv_mc_analytic_mean() to 1e-12 and a brute-force Monte Carlo of 2 million draws at an off-preferred cell.

r.snippet:
# E[1/(rate - g)] for rate ~ U[lo, hi] (or a point when lo == hi). At g = 0
# this is the closed form ln(hi/lo)/(hi - lo).
npv_e_inv_rate <- function(lo, hi, g = 0) {
  if (hi > lo) log((hi - g) / (lo - g)) / (hi - lo) else 1 / (lo - g)
}

# The model's exact expectation for one setting of every input:
#   NPV = q*WT - f*C/(rate - g), WT ~ U[wt_min, wt_max], C ~ U[c_min, c_max],
#   rate ~ U[rate_min, rate_max], mutually independent, with f either implied
#   by WT (SSRN, f_spec = list(mode = "implied", baseline = B): f = 1 - WT/B),
#   an independent uniform (NBER, list(mode = "uniform", lo, hi)), or fixed
#   (list(mode = "fixed", value)). q (litigation survival applied to revenue)
#   and g (growth of the lost income) are 1 and 0 in both scripts as shipped;
#   the explorer moves them (NOTES.md notes 2, 3 and 5). Used by
#   npv_mc_analytic_mean() below and by the explorer grid (R/site.R).
npv_expectation <- function(wt_min, wt_max, c_min, c_max, rate_min, rate_max,
                            f_spec, q = 1, g = 0) {
  e_wt <- (wt_min + wt_max) / 2
  e_f <- switch(f_spec$mode,
    implied = 1 - e_wt / f_spec$baseline,
    uniform = (f_spec$lo + f_spec$hi) / 2,
    fixed   = f_spec$value
  )
  pv_lost <- e_f * mean(c(c_min, c_max)) * npv_e_inv_rate(rate_min, rate_max, g)
  collected <- q * e_wt

layers.name: The draw ranges and the revenue ceiling
layers.what: Where the four ranges come from. The top of the revenue draw, 72, is a literal in the authors' script: revenue if the Act survives, after removing seven confirmed departures. The pipeline rebuilds it from the NBER person-level file final.csv: 5% of each domestic billionaire's grown wealth, summed, minus the seven who left, gives 72.05 (note 4: 72 in the script, 72.06 in the README). The 0 bottom is the Act struck down. The f, C and r ranges are the script's literals; C's ends are the two income tax Monte Carlo bounds of Table 8.

inputs_from.what: the authors' repository: NPV_dist_v8.R (the literals) and final.csv (240 rows)

layers.other_inputs: the C range 3.3 to 5.8 from Table 8 (target income_tax_table8, off this chain)
layers.method_ref: NBER PDF pp.22-23 and the NBER README. Matches with a caveat: the Monte Carlo uses the script's 72, not the recomputed 72.05 (NOTES.md note 4); test-nber-final.R checks both numbers.

extract_nber_final <- function(path = rauh_nber_final_csv()) {
  readr_read_csv <- function(path) {
    df <- utils::read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = TRUE)
    tibble::as_tibble(df)
  }
  readr_read_csv(path)
}

# Domestic total at grown (7%) vintage = the NBER version's "$100.9B face
# value" (NBER README table). Removing the 7 removed_departed rows gives
# the ceiling the README calls "$72.06B" (we recompute 72.05B - see
# NOTES.md note 4). The 7 = SSRN's 6 confirmed departures (Page, Brin,
# Thiel, Hankey, Spielberg, Sacks) plus Travis Kalanick (net worth $3.5B,
# added for the NBER vintage).
compute_nber_ceiling <- function(final_df) {
  dom <- final_df[final_df$panel == "domestic", ]
  intl <- final_df[final_df$panel == "international", ]
  removed <- dom[dom$bucket == "removed_departed", ]

  domestic_total_grown <- sum(dom$face_tax_5pct) / 1e9
  removed_departed_total <- sum(removed$face_tax_5pct) / 1e9
  ceiling_recomputed <- domestic_total_grown - removed_departed_total
  international_net_worth <- sum(intl$net_worth_usd) / 1e9
  # Two subsets of the seven, for the comparison's departures dial: the four the BSZ
  # analysis's aggressive row also removes, at this file's grown taxable value, and the two
  # the BSZ workbook does not list by name, at their net worth.
  four <- c("Larry Page", "Peter Thiel", "Don Hankey", "Travis Kalanick")
  two  <- c("Steven Spielberg", "David Sacks")
  stopifnot(all(c(four, two) %in% removed$name))
  departed_four_grown <- sum(removed$wealth_in_tax_base_usd_7pct[removed$name %in% four]) / 1e9
  spielberg_sacks_net_worth <- sum(removed$net_worth_usd[removed$name %in% two]) / 1e9

  list(
    n_domestic = nrow(dom),
    n_international = nrow(intl),
    n_removed_departed = nrow(removed),
    domestic_total_grown = domestic_total_grown,        # ~100.906 ("$100.9B")
    removed_departed_total = removed_departed_total,     # ~28.854
    ceiling_recomputed = ceiling_recomputed,              # ~72.051 (README says 72.06)
    international_net_worth = international_net_worth,   # ~146.3 ("$146.3B")
    departed_four_grown = departed_four_grown,            # ~314.8 (Page, Thiel, Hankey, Kalanick)
    spielberg_sacks_net_worth = spielberg_sacks_net_worth, # ~9.0
    removed_names = removed$name
  )
}

def extract_nber_final(path):
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        return list(csv.DictReader(f))


def compute_nber_ceiling(final_rows):
    dom = [r for r in final_rows if r["panel"] == "domestic"]
    intl = [r for r in final_rows if r["panel"] == "international"]
    removed = [r for r in dom if r["bucket"] == "removed_departed"]

    def s(rows, key):
        return sum(float(r[key]) for r in rows if r[key] not in ("", None))

    domestic_total_grown = s(dom, "face_tax_5pct") / 1e9
    removed_departed_total = s(removed, "face_tax_5pct") / 1e9
    ceiling_recomputed = domestic_total_grown - removed_departed_total
    international_net_worth = s(intl, "net_worth_usd") / 1e9
    four = ("Larry Page", "Peter Thiel", "Don Hankey", "Travis Kalanick")
    two = ("Steven Spielberg", "David Sacks")
    names = {r["name"] for r in removed}
    assert all(n in names for n in four + two)
    departed_four_grown = s([r for r in removed if r["name"] in four], "wealth_in_tax_base_usd_7pct") / 1e9
    spielberg_sacks_net_worth = s([r for r in removed if r["name"] in two], "net_worth_usd") / 1e9

    return {
        "n_domestic": len(dom),
        "n_international": len(intl),
        "n_removed_departed": len(removed),
        "domestic_total_grown": domestic_total_grown,
        "removed_departed_total": removed_departed_total,
        "ceiling_recomputed": ceiling_recomputed,
        "international_net_worth": international_net_worth,
        "departed_four_grown": departed_four_grown,
        "spielberg_sacks_net_worth": spielberg_sacks_net_worth,
        "removed_names": [r["name"] for r in removed],
    }

r.snippet:
set.seed(2026)
plot_dir <- "../NPV_plots"

# ---- Parameters ----
n_sims <- 100000
wt_min <- 0;    wt_max <- 72      # wealth-tax revenue ($B), embeds litigation range
f_min  <- 0.30; f_max  <- 0.60    # fraction of income-tax base that departs
c_min  <- 3.3;  c_max  <- 5.8     # annual billionaire income tax ($B)
rg_min <- 0.015; rg_max <- 0.045  # net real discount rate (r - g)

# ---- Draws ----
wt <- runif(n_sims, wt_min, wt_max)
f  <- runif(n_sims, f_min,  f_max)
c_income    <- runif(n_sims, c_min,  c_max)
rg_discount <- runif(n_sims, rg_min, rg_max)

# ---- NPV ----
npv <- wt - (f * c_income) / rg_discount
